https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R22.body:
Attention Residents,

To address various traffic matters in a more channelized manner, Lancaster Township is reestablishing its Traffic Committee to provide a more structured approach to reviewing traffic-related concerns. This committee is advisory to the Board of Supervisors and no action beyond recommendations to the Board. The Committee will consist of three Township representatives, or their designees: the Township Manager, Public Works Superintendent, and Chief of Police.

Residents are welcome to attend Traffic Committee meetings; however, attendance is not necessary to have your concerns heard. Residents who are unable to attend, or who prefer to provide comments in advance, may submit them by email to Public Works Superintendent Devin Groff at dgroff@twp.lancaster.pa.us. All submitted comments will be documented and provided to Committee members for consideration.

The Committee Chair may read submitted comments aloud, in whole or in part, during the meeting.

Meetings will be held quarterly on the second Monday of January, April, July, and October at noon, coinciding with the regularly scheduled Board of Supervisors meeting day. Meetings will take place in the meeting room at 1240 Maple Avenue, with entrance access from Perry Avenue. An opportunity for public comment will be provided at the conclusion of each meeting.

https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R22.title: Keep Leaf Piles Off the Street
https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R22.body:
Residents, we are so excited that you're ready for our curbside leaf collection services this year, but they are not scheduled to begin until October 8th! Do not place any leaves in the street. Property owners may be given a notice if this issue persists.

Until October 8th, we operate our biweekly street sweeping program, click here for our Street Operations Calendar . While our sweeper is cleaning the roads, and sometimes that's a few leaves, the sweeper equipment is not designed for leaf picking. The sweeper will go around these piles as they could cause malfunction or equipment breakdowns. Please help us keep the streets as orderly as possible until leaf collection season by using our biweekly yard waste collection using brown bags or bring them by the woody waste facility during operating hours, here is a calendar for Woody Waste .

Keeping the leaves out of the street and disposing of them in yard waste bags or at the woody waste facility will do a few things:
  • Keeps parking lanes more available for vehicles
  • Allows for better street sweeping through the season
  • Prevents leaves washing away and forming stormwater clogs at inlets
The best thing you can do in the tighter neighborhoods with limited areas to store piles off-street, is to bag them in brown bags for yard waste collection or to store until you can make it out to woody waste. It keeps them stored in a way they won't blow around, out of the way, and if you forget to put them out while brown bags get collected until October 8th, you can always take them to Woody Waste and reuse the bag a few times through the season.

Please make sure you are signed up for the Township E-notify system by clicking HERE and that you are familiar with your leaf collection zone by clicking HERE to see the map. We use the alert box to send out leaf collection communications, and now with E-Notify you can get alerted of those changes. We ask residents keep all leaf piles off the street in collection season until 48 hours from communicated service. This practice also helps minimize the above impacts in the thick of the leaf drop. We know this time of year can be a lot to manage; with your help we can manage it well.

If you have any questions, please first direct them to the Communications and Outreach Coordinator, Tony Dastra, by sending an email with your inquiry to pwadmin@twp.lancaster.pa.us . If you click the link, it will prefill the email and subject.

https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R22.title: North Conestoga Drive Closure Notice
https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R22.body:
We are distributing a paper notice to residents along affected roadways. This news item is to serve as a digital copy that residents can share as needed.

Attention Resident,

During the recent flooding in early September, the highwater caused significant erosion along the Conestoga River. A section of the riverbank has separated and failed, extending to the edge of the roadway. Although the pavement has not visibly failed, the erosion may have affected the ground supporting the roadway. At this time, we do not know how far the damage extends beneath the pavement or how stable the roadway is.

For the safety of the public, the affected section of North Conestoga Drive will be closed to through traffic until further notice.

We understand that residents and businesses in the area still need access. The barricades closing the affected section will be positioned to allow local access where possible. Please be aware that traffic will only be able to travel in one direction through the accessible portion of the roadway, and you may need to adjust your normal travel routes. We appreciate your patience and cooperation as we address this sudden and unfortunate situation. Our priority is to protect the safety of residents, businesses, and motorists while we determine the best course of action.

A map showing the upcoming signage and detour route is attached. Please use caution, follow all posted signs, and allow additional time for travel.

If you have questions regarding the closure, please contact the Public Works Superintendent, Devin Groff, at dgroff@twp.lancaster.pa.us.

Thank you for your patience and understanding,

Lancaster Township Communications

Estimado residente,

Durante las recientes inundaciones de principios de septiembre, el nivel elevado del agua provocó una erosión significativa a lo largo del río Conestoga. Un tramo de la ribera ha cedido y se ha desprendido, extendiéndose hasta el borde de la calzada. Aunque el pavimento no presenta daños visibles, la erosión podría haber afectado el terreno que sirve de base a la carretera. Por el momento, desconocemos el alcance de los daños bajo el pavimento o el grado de estabilidad de la vía.

Por seguridad pública, el tramo afectado de North Conestoga Drive permanecerá cerrado al tráfico de paso hasta nuevo aviso.

Entendemos que los residentes y negocios de la zona necesitan seguir teniendo acceso. Las barreras que cierran el tramo afectado se colocarán de manera que permitan el acceso local siempre que sea posible. Tenga en cuenta que la circulación por la parte accesible de la vía será de sentido único, por lo que es posible que deba modificar sus rutas habituales. Agradecemos su paciencia y colaboración mientras gestionamos esta situación imprevista y desafortunada. Nuestra prioridad es proteger la seguridad de los residentes, los negocios y los conductores mientras determinamos la mejor forma de proceder.

Se adjunta un mapa con la señalización prevista y la ruta de desvío. Le rogamos que extreme las precauciones, respete todas las señales y prevea tiempo adicional para sus desplazamientos.

Si tiene alguna pregunta sobre el cierre, puede ponerse en contacto con el Superintendente de Obras Públicas, Devin Groff, en la dirección dgroff@twp.lancaster.pa.us.

Gracias por su paciencia y comprensión.

https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R19.title: No Mow May... Not Okay!
https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R19.body:
Dear Lancaster Township Residents,

We love how ecologically-minded you are. Recently, our Board of Supervisors passed changes to our Grass and Weeds Ordinance to further promote the biodiversity of our community, However, we need to debunk a myth, and make one thing clear… No Mow May, is NOT OKAY! It might even be doing harm to the local ecosystem at large.

What started with good intentions as a community trend, has been debunked. Native plants and a shift in land stewardship practices for property owners, away from the common well-manicured lawn, have demonstrated themselves to be a positive force for our pollinators, however, typically people who are practicing No Mow May are allowing their non-native, or even invasive, turfgrasses and weeds to grow during the month of May to a problematic degree. It is a huge reason for the positive ordinance changes to allow for Naturalized Landscape exceptions, and we will be educating residents on those in the coming months through online resources, but in the interim, we must insist that residents who still have turfgrass continue to mow and maintain their lawns to the required six inches or less to prevent seeding and spreading which can impact our waterways and neighbors. We send around inspectors on a weekly basis, and we will be enforcing maintenance requirements on weeds and turfgrasses.

If you have any questions about No Mow May itself, please read this Q&A from PennState Extension, one of the places where we get information from to help aid our residents on these practices. For any additional questions, feel free to send an email to our Communication and Outreach Coordinator, Tony Dastra, at pwadmin@twp.lancaster.pa.us.

Thank you for your cooperation and understanding!

https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R19.title: Kittens Rescued! Bottle-feeding Foster Needed!
https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R19.body:
It all started with picking up a plastic bag...

Hello residents, this is Tony Dastra, your Communications and Outreach Coordinator for Lancaster Township. This morning, I was outside performing our first round of outdoor maintenance inspections for the year, reminder to mow your lawns. After having a serendipitous conversation about our plastic bag ordinance with some residents, I continued on to Hamilton Road and spotted a plastic bag beside a storm inlet. I went to pick up the trash, but what I found was WAY MORE than a plastic bag.

The bag had pet food in it, and that confused me. Why is there pet food by a storm inlet? Well, upon further inspection, I found a bowl, a blanket, and a small little animal that was not moving. I was distraught, and so were some residents who saw all this happen in real time. As I continued investigating the situation… I heard something… little meows. What I thought was a very dim circumstance, was now becoming an active rescue with a lot of hope.

I made some calls, and Sgt. Carpenter arrived on the scene to lend a hand. We were able to remove the inlet top safely, and in addition to the little animal in the leaf litter, spotted four kittens a few feet inside the storm pipe. Not only that, the little one that I originally thought to be deceased, WAS ALIVE. We had FIVE live baby cats on our hands!

Sgt. Carpenter and I were able to get them out safely with the support of some nearby residents. I’m happy to report they were taken to the emergency vet for treatment, and all are in decent health considering the circumstances with a shot at becoming big strong cats. we are so thankful to Sgt. Carpenter from the Lancaster Township Police Department, and every resident who stopped to lend a hand, however, WE STILL NEED HELP! They are so young that they need someone willing to foster and bottle feed them. We have some basic items to get the care started, and we have some info on how to care for them. We are looking for someone to help us with this ongoing effort. If you are interested or know somebody, call (223)221-7520. Thank you!

Tony Dastra, Communication and Outreach Coordinator for Lancaster Township

https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R18.title: Mosquito Spraying on September 4th
https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R18.body:
Attention Township Residents,

The Mosquito-borne Disease Control Program Coordinator for Lancaster County has put out a press release to inform our residents of the spraying set to occur between sunset and 10PM in Lancaster Township and parts of neighboring communities. They do ask people to remain inside during this treatment, and outdoor activity can occur after 30 minutes. If you have more questions, contact information can be found at the end of this release. 

Thank you,
Lancaster Township Communications

FULL PRESS RELEASE
West Nile Virus ULV Truck Spray in Lancaster County 09/04


Hello, 

There is a truck-mounted ULV spray to control mosquito populations in Lancaster County scheduled for Thursday, September 4th. Parts of East Hempfield Township, Lancaster Township, and Lancaster City will be affected. Please share the following press release with residents: 

"East Hempfield Township, Lancaster Township, and Lancaster City, Pa. (September 4th, 2025) –

Residential and recreational areas in and around Noel Dorwart Park, Spring Valley Road and Mimosa Lane, Riverside Avenue, E. Orange Avenue, Clark Street, Hawthorne Ridge, Conestoga Memorial Park, Brandon Park, Full Circle Recycling on S. Prince Street, St. Mary’s Cemetery, Stauffer Park, and N. Plum Street will be sprayed for adult mosquitoes beginning around sunset (7:35 pm) on September 4th. Please keep in mind that the roads listed are for reference and other roads and areas in close proximity may be sprayed as well. We ask that residents remain inside while the spray is being conducted, though outside activities may resume 30 minutes after the spray. As a common courtesy we turn off the sprayer when passing by people, but this intermission in the application alters the drift of the product which disrupts a steady, even application and may be less effective. The spray will conclude by 10:00 pm.

High populations of adult mosquitoes that vector West Nile Virus to humans have been detected in these areas. Weather conditions and other unexpected events could delay or cancel the spray operation. If these operations are cancelled, they will be rescheduled for September 8th.

The Lancaster and Lebanon County Mosquito and Tick-Borne Disease Control Specialist and a Department of Environmental Protection biologist will be on site for the application. The Lancaster and Lebanon Mosquito-Borne Disease Program will be conducting this truck-mounted ultra-low volume (ULV) mosquito control operation using the Lancaster County truck under business license BU 9444, and the product used will be Aquaduet applied at a rate of 1.0 fluid oz/acre. This product is designed to provide quick knockdown and effective control of adult mosquitoes. The control event is performed by way of an Ultra-Low Volume Truck Mounted Spray. Our sprayer puts out the product in microscopic droplets (approximately a shot glass of product is applied over the distance of a football field). Because the droplets are so small, they degrade quickly and are only “potent” for roughly 20 minutes before they begin to degrade. Therefore, it is unable to adhere to vegetation/surfaces or leech into groundwater. This protects non-target species such as pollinators and aquatic life. Additionally, we specifically deploy this product after dusk when the target mosquito species is most active and pollinators are not. We understand the role pollinators play, and we want to ensure that we do them no harm while also protecting public health from potential mosquito-borne diseases.

Lancaster County residents should protect themselves from mosquito bites by wearing or implementing some form of repellent, including wearing long sleeves and pants when outside. Additionally, residents and homeowners should be vigilant of standing water, including artificial containers holding water such as buckets, clogged gutters, unmaintained pools, or tarps. Eliminate all sources of standing water from your property. Something as small as a soda bottle cap filled with water can breed mosquitoes.

For more information, contact the Lancaster and Lebanon County Mosquito and Tick-Borne Disease Control Specialist Lydia Mohn at 717-277-5275 x 112 or lydia.mohn@lccd.org."

From,

Lydia Mohn
Mosquito-borne Disease Control Program Coordinator – Lebanon & Lancaster Counties
Lebanon County Conservation District
Office phone: 717-277-5275 x112
www.lccd.org/mosquito-borne-disease-program

https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R16.body:
Attention Residents and Lancaster Township Property Owners,

Lancaster County will undergo a property reassessment over the next couple years to take effect in 2027, the first since 2018, to ensure all property values align with current fair market values. This reassessment is part of the county’s eight-year cycle and is designed to fairly distribute property tax burdens across all properties.

What Does This Mean for Property Owners?

A reassessment does not automatically mean higher taxes. By Pennsylvania law, taxing jurisdictions—such as the county, municipality, and school district—must adjust their millage rates in a reassessment year to be revenue neutral. While taxing bodies may later adjust their rates through a separate vote, any increase is capped at 10% of the previous year’s total tax revenue. However, individual property taxes may rise or fall based on how a property’s reassessed value compares to others in the community.

How Are New Property Values Determined?

Lancaster County’s reassessment is conducted in-house using certified Pennsylvania Evaluators (CPEs) who analyze recent sales trends and market studies. Fair market value is determined through legitimate real estate transactions, ensuring that properties of similar types and locations are assessed equitably.

Available Tax Relief Programs

Homeowners may be eligible for tax relief programs, including:

  • Senior Citizen Rent Rebate Program – Contact the Office of Aging at 1-800-801-3070 or visit lancoaging.org.
  • Disabled Veterans Assistance – Learn more at the Department of Military and Veteran Affairs by calling 1-800-547-2838 or visiting lancastercountypa.gov.
  • Clean & Green Program – A tax reduction initiative for agricultural and open land. Visit lancastercountypa.gov for details.
  • Homestead/Farmstead Exclusion – Offers property tax reductions for owner-occupied properties. More information can be found at lancastercountypa.gov.

For more details on the 2027 reassessment process, visit the Lancaster County Property Assessment Office website.

https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R11.title: Removing English Ivy: Very Demure, Very Mindful
https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R11.body:
English Ivy, with its lush greenery and rapid growth, has long been a popular choice for groundcover and decorative climbing. However, once this invasive vine leaves the ground, it poses significant threats to both the environment and buildings.

As English Ivy climbs trees and structures, it begins to produce fruits containing seeds that are easily spread by wildlife. This allows the plant to aggressively invade new areas, often unnoticed until it's too late. The ivy can smother and kill trees, turning them into dangerous falling hazards, while also damaging buildings by extracting nutrients from mortar and compromising structural integrity.


Given these risks, it’s essential to act. Killing the English Ivy on trees, buildings, and other structures is crucial to prevent further damage and protect our ecosystems. Removal of a live vine is not recommended because pulling it could bring whatever it is attached to. They will sloth off so long as they are cut away from the root; it is recommended to remove only a one-foot section.

This invasive plant should be carefully eradicated wherever it’s found, and ongoing vigilance is necessary to prevent its return. Removing English Ivy from your property is a proactive step that safeguards our environments from serious harm. If you still want that climbing vine aesthetic replace English Ivy with Virginia Creeper, Parthenocissus quinquefolia, a similar native choice that is less damaging to trees and buildings or consider other native or non-invasive species of vines such as Celastrus scandens, Campsis radicans, Clematis virginiana, Lonicera sempervirens.

Lancaster Township Historical Commission
Historical Marker Unveiling Ceremony
Wabank Road and Pilgrim Drive
November 17, 2022 – 3:00 pm

Lancaster Township invites you to an unveiling ceremony of an historical marker being erected by the Township Historical Commission and Public Works Department.

The marker commemorates the long-ago presence of a village of indigenous people who occupied this area before those whom we today refer to as the “Conestoga Indians” and the “Susquehannock.” The modern-day name “Shenks Ferry People” was attributed to these earliest farmers of Lancaster County, because it was there that archaeologists first discovered evidence of this culture.

Predating contact with White Europeans, all that has been documented about the Shenk’s Ferry People is based on excavation sites, such as the one here and near Millersville University. More information can be found at this link.

https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R13.title: Public Notice for City Water Customers
https://www.twp.lancaster.pa.us/_T22_R13.body:
Attention Township Residents who are City Water Customers,

The City of Lancaster's water system recently detected levels of Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) in the drinking water that exceed the Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) set by regulatory standards. This is not an emergency, but as a resident, it's important to be informed about the situation and what is being done to address it.

What Happened?

On September 13, 2024, routine water testing revealed PFOA levels at 16 ng/L, which is above the MCL of 14 ng/L. The elevated levels of PFOA were found in finished water from the Conestoga Treatment Plant, which sources water from the Conestoga River. However, water from the Susquehanna Treatment Plant has no detectable levels of PFOA or other perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

The City of Lancaster is actively investigating the elevated levels and making adjustments to the water treatment process at the Conestoga Plant. The issue is expected to be resolved within 12 months.

What Should You Do?

  • You do not need to switch to bottled water or use alternative water sources.
  • If you have specific health concerns, you may want to consult your doctor.

What Does This Mean?

Although this is not an immediate health risk, long-term exposure to PFOA above the MCL can potentially cause adverse health effects, such as developmental issues and immune response problems.

Understanding PFOS and PFOA

PFOA and Perfluorooctane Sulfonate (PFOS) are part of a group of man-made chemicals known as PFAS. These substances have been widely used in industrial applications, firefighting foams, and consumer products like non-stick cookware, carpets, and packaging. They are resistant to heat, water, and oil, and persist both in the environment and in the human body. Most people are exposed to PFAS through various sources, not just drinking water.

Further Information

Residents are encouraged to stay informed by visiting the City of Lancaster’s website or contacting the Water Quality Laboratory at 717-291-4818 for more details.

Please share this information with others, especially those who may not have received this notice directly, such as people in apartments, nursing homes, schools, and businesses. This news item was adapted from a public notice that was mailed out to City water customers. We are just reiterating the information to make sure residents are aware.

Thank you for your attention,

Lancaster Township Communications Team
